title: Single Sign-on / Federated Access
description: How single sign-on (Kerberos, Sesame) and federated identity management (trust relationships, SAML, WS-Federation, OpenID, OAuth) let users access many systems with one login.

nodes.title: Allows users to access multiple systems with a single set of credentials
nodes.description:
What single sign-on and federated identity management have in common: both let users access multiple systems with one set of credentials.
Users love this: they remember one terrible password instead of many, and authenticate once to get access to all their applications.

children.title: Single Sign-on
children.description:
Access systems within the same organization.
Single sign-on protocols and systems are designed to work within one organization.

children.title: Kerberos
children.description:
A major protocol that enables single sign-on.
Authenticates users with tickets over an insecure network.

children.title: Components
children.description: Kerberos is a complicated, very flexible protocol, so it has many components.

children.title: User / Client
children.description: The person who wants to access services through Kerberos.

children.title: Key Distribution Center
children.description: The KDC. Contains the two services Kerberos provides: the Authentication Service and the Ticket Granting Service.

children.title: Authentication Service
children.description:
To access a service through Kerberos, the user first authenticates with the Authentication Service.
It checks that the user exists. If so, it sends the user two tickets, one of which is the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).

children.title: Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)
children.description: The user passes the TGT to the Ticket Granting Service, the other component in the KDC, with a couple of messages saying which service the user wants to access.

children.title: Ticket Granting Service
children.description:
Checks that the requested service exists and that the user is authorized to access it.
If so, it creates a Service Ticket and sends it to the user.

children.title: Service Tickets
children.description:
What the user finally sends to the application to get access to it.
The user caches the Service Ticket for future access, while the ticket is valid and not expired.

children.title: Service
children.description: The application the user wants to access. The user presents a Service Ticket to it to get access.

children.title: Symmetric encryption only
children.description:
By default, Kerberos supports only symmetric key cryptography.
A significant limitation: quite a few symmetric keys may need to be created and securely distributed among the components.

children.title: Sesame
children.description:
Another single sign-on protocol: the Secure European System for Applications in a Multi-vendor Environment.
Unlike Kerberos, it supports asymmetric cryptography too.

children.title: Symmetric & Asymmetric encryption
children.description:
Sesame supports asymmetric cryptography as well as symmetric.
This solves the major problems of symmetric key cryptography: scalability and key distribution.

children.title: Federated Identity Management (FIM)
children.description:
Access systems across multiple entities.
To the user it looks exactly like single sign-on: enter one set of credentials and get access to many applications.
The key difference: with federated access, users can access not only internal applications, but also externally managed ones, such as SaaS applications in the cloud.

children.title: Trust Relationship
children.description:
Federated access relies on a trust relationship between three entities: the user, the identity provider and the service provider.
The service provider must trust the authentication done by the identity provider before it authorizes the user to access the service.

children.title: Principal / User
children.description: The user, sometimes also called the principal.

children.title: Identity Provider
children.description:
Authenticates the user: verifies the user's identity by knowledge, ownership or characteristic.
In many organizations, the identity provider is something like Active Directory.

children.title: Relying Party / Service Provider
children.description:
What the user wants to access. The service provider is sometimes also called the relying party.
Often not owned by the organization, but owned and managed by a vendor. Example: SaaS applications used at work to submit help desk tickets, book travel or enter expenses.

children.title: SAML
children.description:
Security Assertion Markup Language.
Several protocols enable federated access. SAML is the major one you need to know.

children.title: Tokens
children.description: Kerberos sends tickets. SAML does the same thing, but calls them tokens.

children.title: Assertions written in XML
children.description:
Tokens contain assertion statements, such as the user ID, the service ID, and the timestamp and lifetime of the token.
The assertion statements are written in XML (Extensible Markup Language).

children.title: Components
children.description: SAML was designed for many different use cases, so it is made of several components that make it flexible and adaptable.

children.title: Profiles
children.description: Define how SAML can be used for different business use cases, such as web single sign-on or through LDAP.

children.title: Bindings
children.description: Map SAML onto different communication protocols, such as HTTP, so SAML can communicate across different types of networks.

children.title: Protocol
children.description: Defines how entities send and respond to requests.

children.title: Assertion
children.description: Defines the authentication, authorization and other attributes.

children.title: WS-Federation
children.description: A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides both authentication and authorization.

children.title: OpenID
children.description: A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides authentication.

children.title: OAuth
children.description: A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides authorization.
